reigns.tagline: The would-be philosopher king who died in his bath
reigns.previously: Constantine VIII dies, after forcing Romanos Argyros to marry Zoe.
paragraphs: Romanos was rich, well born and fond of books. Psellos says he saw himself as a new Marcus Aurelius and wanted to found a dynasty. He tried ointments, charms and potions so that Zoe, around 50, might still give him a son. Nothing worked, and he soon lost interest in her and kept her short of money.

He wanted military glory too. In 1030 he led a huge army against Aleppo, but it panicked when it was ambushed in the hot Syrian summer, and the emperor himself barely escaped. His general George Maniakes made up for it in 1031 by capturing Edessa. At home Romanos spent heavily on his great new monastery of the Peribleptos and squeezed the taxpayers to pay for it.

Zoe, ignored, fell for a strikingly good-looking young man from Paphlagonia called Michael, brought to court by his brother John, a powerful eunuch. Romanos was warned and refused to believe it. On 11 April 1034 he was found dying in his bath. That same night Zoe married Michael and had him crowned.

claims.text: Romanos III was drowned in his bath on the orders of Zoe and Michael.
claims.note: Psellos, who saw the body, strongly hints at it, and later chroniclers repeat it as fact. Nobody was ever tried.

claims.text: He was slowly poisoned for months before he died.
claims.note: Psellos and Skylitzes both mention a long wasting illness that some blamed on poison. It can't be proved.

claims.text: George Maniakes captured Edessa in 1031.
claims.note: Skylitzes records it. Maniakes also sent home the letter Christ was said to have written to King Abgar of Edessa.

reigns.hook: Zoe has a new husband, Michael, about 24 and very handsome. But behind him stands his brother John, a eunuch with ideas of his own, and Michael has a secret illness.

reigns.tagline: The empress's toy boy turned dying soldier
reigns.cameToPower: Married Zoe the night Romanos died
reigns.previously: Romanos III is found dead in his bath. Zoe marries her lover Michael.
paragraphs: Michael came from a humble family in Paphlagonia, on the Black Sea coast. His brother John, a eunuch who ran the great orphanage of Constantinople, had got him a post at court, and Zoe did the rest. Once Michael was emperor, John took over the government, and Zoe found herself watched and fenced in by the brothers she had made powerful.

Michael had epilepsy. During his fits, Psellos says, curtains were drawn round him so no one would see. Yet he worked hard and took his job seriously. The tall Norwegian Harald Hardrada served in his Varangian Guard, and in 1038 George Maniakes landed in Sicily to take it back from the Arabs, winning Messina and Syracuse before he was recalled in a quarrel.

In 1040 the Bulgarians rose under Peter Delyan, who claimed to be a grandson of their old tsar Samuel. Michael, now swollen with dropsy, insisted on leading the army himself, and in 1041 he crushed the revolt and came home in triumph. Weeks later, dying, he became a monk. When Zoe came to see him he refused to let her in. He died on 10 December 1041.

claims.text: Michael IV suffered from epilepsy.
claims.note: Psellos, who served at his court, describes his seizures in detail. Skylitzes agrees.

claims.text: Harald Hardrada, later king of Norway, served in the Varangian Guard.
claims.note: The Norse sagas tell it at length, and the Byzantine writer Kekaumenos confirms that "Araltes" served the emperors.

claims.text: Dying, Michael refused to see Zoe when she came to him.
claims.note: Psellos tells it. He liked Michael but may have sharpened the scene for effect.

reigns.hook: Michael IV dies a monk. Zoe has already adopted his nephew, also called Michael, the son of a ship's caulker. John the eunuch thinks the boy will obey him. He is very wrong.

reigns.tagline: The caulker's son who threw out the empress
reigns.previously: Michael IV dies a monk. Zoe's adopted son, his nephew, steps up.
paragraphs: Michael's father had caulked ships for a living, so the city nicknamed the young man Kalaphates, "the Caulker". His uncles had pushed Zoe into adopting him, and he swore to treat her as his mother and mistress. Within weeks he turned on the family that made him. He packed off his powerful uncle, the eunuch John the Orphanotrophos, to exile.

Then he went for Zoe herself. On the night of 18 April 1042 he had her shorn as a nun and shipped to an island in the Sea of Marmara. He had badly misjudged the city. Zoe was Basil II's niece, born in the purple, and people loved the old dynasty. Crowds poured into the streets, attacked his relatives' houses and stormed towards the palace.

Michael hurried Zoe back and showed her to the crowd, but it was too late. Her sister Theodora was fetched from her convent and proclaimed in Hagia Sophia. Michael fled by boat with his uncle Constantine to the Stoudios monastery. On 21 April they were dragged out and blinded in the street. Michael lived out his last months as a monk.

claims.text: Michael Psellos watched the blinding of Michael V and his uncle with his own eyes.
claims.note: Psellos was a young court secretary and describes the scene at Stoudios as an eyewitness in his Chronographia.

claims.text: About 3,000 people died in the fighting of April 1042.
claims.note: The figure comes from Skylitzes. Chroniclers' casualty numbers are often rough guesses.

claims.text: His nickname came from his father's old trade of caulking ships.
claims.note: Psellos and Skylitzes both say the family had worked in the shipyards before their rise.

reigns.hook: Michael V is blind and finished. For the first time ever, two sisters, Zoe and Theodora, sit side by side on the throne. They can't stand each other.

reigns.title: Zoe and Theodora
reigns.tagline: Two sisters, one throne, no love lost
reigns.previously: The city rises; Michael V is blinded and Zoe is brought back.
paragraphs: Zoe and Theodora were the last of Basil I's line, the daughters of Constantine VIII. Zoe, the elder, was about 64 and still vain about her looks. Theodora had spent years shut in a convent, partly thanks to her sister. Now the crowd that had toppled Michael V wanted them both, and for the first time in the empire's history two women ruled together.

For seven weeks it more or less worked. They held audiences side by side, sacked Michael's men and gave out justice. Psellos watched them closely. Zoe, he says, turned her rooms into a perfume workshop and kept a face without a wrinkle. She was generous to a fault. Theodora was sharper, plainer and tight with money.

It could not last. The sisters disliked each other, and the court split behind them. Zoe settled it in her own way: she would marry again. Her choice was an old flame, Constantine Monomachos, a charming aristocrat living in exile on Lesbos.

claims.text: Zoe still had a smooth, unlined face in her sixties.
claims.note: Psellos saw her often, but a courtier's flattery is hard to separate from fact.

claims.text: Zoe boiled up perfumes and ointments in her private rooms.
claims.note: Psellos describes the braziers and jars he saw there.

claims.text: This was the only time two women ruled the empire jointly.
claims.note: No other pair of empresses ever ruled together in their own right.

reigns.hook: Zoe is 64 and about to marry for the third time. Her new husband is coming back from exile, and he's bringing his mistress with him.

reigns.tagline: The pleasure-loving emperor of the Great Schism
reigns.previously: Zoe and Theodora rule for seven weeks. Zoe picks a third husband.
paragraphs: Constantine Monomachos was handsome, witty and fond of a good time. He married Zoe on 11 June 1042, then brought in his mistress, Maria Skleraina, gave her a title and rooms in the palace, and the three of them lived together. Zoe seemed not to mind. The people did: in 1044 a crowd rioted, shouting that they wanted no Skleraina as empress.

Trouble came from every side. The great general George Maniakes rebelled in 1043 and was killed at the moment of victory. A Rus fleet attacked the same year and was beaten off. In 1045 Constantine annexed the Armenian kingdom of Ani. In 1047 the rebel Leo Tornikios besieged the capital and nearly got in. Constantine also founded a law school, run by Psellos's friend John Xiphilinos.

Zoe died in 1050. In 1054 a row with Rome boiled over. On 16 July the papal envoy Cardinal Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch Michael Keroularios hit back in kind. That split, the Great Schism, still divides the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Constantine died in January 1055.

claims.text: Maria Skleraina lived openly in the palace with an official title.
claims.note: Psellos, who served Constantine, describes the arrangement closely. Her title was sebaste.

claims.text: Humbert laid the bull on the altar of Hagia Sophia on 16 July 1054.
claims.note: Recorded in both Greek and Latin documents from the time.

claims.text: In the Hagia Sophia mosaic, Constantine's face replaced an earlier husband's.
claims.note: The heads and his name were clearly altered. Many think it first showed Romanos III, but nobody can be sure.

reigns.hook: Constantine IX is dead. His advisers have picked a successor, but old Theodora, last of the Macedonians, is not finished yet.

reigns.tagline: The spinster empress who closed a 190-year dynasty
reigns.previously: Constantine IX dies in 1055, months after the Great Schism.
paragraphs: Theodora had spent much of her life in convents and in her sister's shadow. After sharing the throne with Zoe for a few weeks in 1042, she stepped back. As Constantine IX lay dying, his advisers planned to pass the crown to Nikephoros Proteuon, the governor of Bulgaria. Theodora moved first. Her supporters got her to the Great Palace and she was proclaimed empress.

In her seventies and unmarried, she ruled alone and would not take a husband. She worked through trusted officials, chiefly her minister Leo Paraspondylos, and made appointments herself, even in the Church. Psellos grumbled that it was unnatural for a woman to rule, but the empire was quiet.

In August 1056 she fell ill. On her deathbed her advisers had her name an elderly official, Michael Bringas, as her successor. She died on 31 August 1056. The dynasty that Basil the groom had founded almost 190 years earlier was over.

claims.text: Theodora barely took part in choosing Michael VI; her inner circle did it.
claims.note: Psellos says the decision was made by her advisers while she was too ill to speak.

claims.text: She was the last ruler descended from Basil I.
claims.note: With her death the Macedonian dynasty ended, and no one else had a hereditary claim.

reigns.hook: Theodora is dead and her dynasty with her. The new emperor, Michael VI, is an old civil servant, and the generals are running out of patience.

reigns.tagline: The old pen-pusher who scolded his generals
reigns.previously: Old Theodora dies, naming the elderly official Michael Bringas.
paragraphs: Michael Bringas was a lifelong civil servant who had run the army's finances, which earned him the nickname Stratiotikos, "the military one". Theodora's advisers picked him because he seemed safe and pliable. Almost at once a cousin of Constantine IX tried to grab the throne, failed, and was sent into exile.

At Easter 1057 the top generals, Isaac Komnenos and Katakalon Kekaumenos among them, came to court hoping for honours. Michael gave them nothing and scolded them in front of everyone. They went off and plotted in Hagia Sophia. In June 1057 the eastern army proclaimed Isaac emperor, and in August it smashed Michael's loyal troops near Nicaea.

Michael sent Psellos to Isaac's camp to offer him the title of Caesar. While the talks went on, the patriarch Michael Keroularios and his allies in the capital came out for Isaac. With the city against him, Michael VI gave up on 31 August 1057 and became a monk. He lived quietly for about two more years.

claims.text: Michael VI publicly humiliated the generals at Easter 1057, driving them to revolt.
claims.note: Psellos was at court and tells the story. He liked to put himself at the centre of events, but Skylitzes agrees on the snub.

claims.text: Psellos went as Michael's envoy to Isaac's camp.
claims.note: Psellos describes his own embassy at length, though he tends to make himself look clever and loyal to everyone.

reigns.hook: Michael VI swaps his crown for a monk's habit. The soldier Isaac Komnenos rides into the city as emperor, determined to fix the empty treasury fast.

reigns.tagline: The first Komnenos, who held his sword out on his coins
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed by the army in revolt
reigns.previously: Michael VI abdicates and becomes a monk. The generals have won.
paragraphs: Isaac Komnenos was a hard, silent soldier from a family of eastern landowners, brought up as a boy under Basil II's eye. He was crowned on 1 September 1057. He wanted money for the army, and he wanted it fast. He cancelled pensions and gifts handed out by earlier emperors, took back estates, and even laid hands on church property. His gold coins showed him standing with a drawn sword.

The patriarch Michael Keroularios had helped put him on the throne and expected to be thanked for it. Isaac had him arrested in November 1058 and shipped off to an island, and Psellos wrote the charges for a trial. The old patriarch died before it could open, and the crowds turned him into a martyr. In 1059 Isaac campaigned in the Balkans against the Hungarians and Pecheneg nomads.

Back home he fell ill with a fever. Fearing death, he abdicated on 22 November 1059 and became a monk at the Stoudios monastery. He passed over his own family and named Constantine Doukas, a rich aristocrat and Psellos's friend. Isaac lived on as a monk for about a year.

claims.text: Isaac's sword-holding coins meant he credited his throne to his own blade, not to God.
claims.note: The coins are real. The boastful meaning is how later chroniclers read them; it may just be a soldier's image.

claims.text: Isaac offered the crown to his brother John, who turned it down, to the fury of John's wife Anna Dalassene.
claims.note: Told by Nikephoros Bryennios, who married into the family and wrote decades later. Psellos does not mention it.

claims.text: Keroularios died before he could be tried.
claims.note: Psellos, who drafted the accusation, and Attaleiates both record his death in exile early in 1059.

reigns.hook: Isaac retires to the Stoudios monastery. His choice is Constantine Doukas, a rich courtier and Psellos's friend, who thinks the army costs far too much.

reigns.tagline: He saved money on soldiers while the Turks closed in
reigns.previously: Isaac I falls ill, abdicates and enters the Stoudios monastery.
paragraphs: Constantine Doukas came from a great landowning family and had backed Isaac's revolt. His second wife, Eudokia Makrembolitissa, was a niece of the patriarch Keroularios. As emperor he leaned on the senate, the lawyers and the palace officials. Psellos, who had pushed for him, became his closest adviser and tutor to his son Michael.

He loved hearing law cases and hated paying soldiers. Army pay was cut and frontier troops were left to rot. The cost soon showed. In 1064 the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan took Ani, the great Armenian city, and that autumn the Uzes, nomads from the steppe, crossed the Danube in huge numbers. Disease and the winter destroyed them more than any army did. In 1061 Constantine survived a plot to kill him.

He fell ill in 1066. Before he died he made Eudokia swear in writing never to remarry, so that their sons' rights would be safe, and his brother, the Caesar John Doukas, would keep watch. Constantine X died on 23 May 1067. Eudokia took charge for the boys.

claims.text: Eudokia swore in writing never to remarry, to protect her sons' rights.
claims.note: Psellos and other writers mention the oath, which was lodged with the patriarch. She broke it within months.

claims.text: Constantine's cuts left the eastern frontier defenceless.
claims.note: Attaleiates, a soldier's friend, blames him bitterly. Some historians think the army's decline had deeper roots.

reigns.hook: Constantine X is dead. Eudokia has sworn not to remarry. But the Turks are raiding deep into Anatolia, and in a cell sits a handsome general condemned for plotting.

paragraphs: Eudokia ruled as empress for her sons after her husband Constantine X died. He had made her swear never to remarry, to keep the throne safe for his family.

With the Seljuk Turks raiding Anatolia, she broke the oath and married the general Romanos Diogenes on New Year's Day 1068, making him emperor. After his defeat at Manzikert in 1071 she briefly ruled again before being sent to a convent.

reigns.tagline: The emperor the sultan stepped on, then sent home
reigns.previously: Constantine X dies. His widow Eudokia rules for their young sons.
paragraphs: Romanos Diogenes was a tough Cappadocian general who had been sentenced for plotting against Eudokia's sons. She pardoned him, broke her oath and married him on 1 January 1068. The Doukas family, led by Constantine X's brother John, the Caesar, never forgave either of them. Romanos set about rebuilding a neglected army and led it east against the Turks.

In 1071 he marched a huge, patchy army to Manzikert, near Lake Van, to meet Sultan Alp Arslan. On 26 August, as the line pulled back at dusk, the rearguard under Andronikos Doukas, the Caesar's son, marched off the field. Romanos fought on until he was wounded and taken. Brought before the sultan, he was treated with honour and freed after about a week, with a treaty.

He came home to find himself deposed. The Doukas clan had crowned Eudokia's son as Michael VII. Romanos fought and lost, then surrendered on a sworn promise of safety. In 1072 he was blinded anyway, and died of the wounds in a monastery on the island of Prote.

claims.text: Andronikos Doukas betrayed Romanos on purpose at Manzikert.
claims.note: Attaleiates, who was there, says the rearguard spread a rumour the emperor had lost. Whether it was a planned betrayal is argued.

claims.text: Alp Arslan put his foot on the captured emperor's neck, then raised him up and treated him kindly.
claims.note: The foot on the neck was a ritual of triumph described by Muslim writers. Byzantine sources stress the kindness. The details vary a lot.

claims.text: Psellos wrote to the blinded Romanos calling him blessed, as if losing his eyes were a gift from God.
claims.note: A letter of Psellos to Romanos survives; how cruel or sincere it was is debated. Psellos backed the Doukas side.

reigns.hook: Romanos is blind and dying. In the capital, Psellos's star pupil Michael VII sits on the throne, and the Turks have learned that nobody is guarding Anatolia.

reigns.tagline: Psellos's pupil, and a coin that shrank under him
reigns.cameToPower: Put in power by his uncle John
reigns.previously: Romanos is beaten at Manzikert, and the Doukas clan seizes the throne.
paragraphs: Michael was Constantine X's eldest son and Psellos's star pupil, bookish and fond of poetry. When news came that Romanos IV had been captured at Manzikert, his uncle the Caesar John Doukas and Psellos had Michael proclaimed sole emperor and packed Eudokia off to a convent. Romanos came back to fight for his crown, lost, and was blinded in 1072.

The real power was a eunuch minister, Nikephoritzes, who squeezed everyone and set up a state grain monopoly. Prices climbed and the gold coin got lighter, so people called Michael Parapinakes, "minus a quarter". The Norman mercenary Roussel de Bailleul rebelled and even made the Caesar John a puppet emperor, until the young Alexios Komnenos caught him with a Turkish chief's help.

Turkish bands spread across Anatolia. In late 1077 two generals named Nikephoros revolted: Bryennios in the Balkans and Botaneiates in Anatolia. Riots broke out in the capital and Nikephoritzes fled. On 31 March 1078 Michael gave up the throne and became a monk at Stoudios. He was later made archbishop of Ephesus.

claims.text: The nickname Parapinakes came from the coin buying a quarter-measure less wheat.
claims.note: Chroniclers explain it this way, and the coin was being debased while grain prices rose.

claims.text: Michael's son Constantine was engaged to a daughter of the Norman Robert Guiscard.
claims.note: The match was agreed in 1074 and the girl was sent to Constantinople; Anna Komnene and other writers record it.

claims.text: Michael was a model philosopher-king.
claims.note: That is Psellos's verdict on his own pupil. Other writers saw a weak ruler who left the state to Nikephoritzes.

reigns.hook: Michael VII swaps his crown for a monk's habit. Old Nikephoros Botaneiates rides in from Anatolia to take the throne, and he has his eye on Michael's wife too.

reigns.tagline: An old general who took the throne and the queen
reigns.previously: Michael VII gives up the throne and becomes a monk at Stoudios.
paragraphs: Nikephoros Botaneiates was a veteran general who claimed descent from the great Phokas family. His troops proclaimed him in January 1078, and he moved on the capital with Turkish help. When Michael VII abdicated, the city opened its gates. He then married Michael's wife, the beautiful Maria of Alania, although Michael was still alive. The Church was scandalised.

He was generous with titles and gifts, and the treasury ran dry. His best general was young Alexios Komnenos, who beat the rebel Bryennios and then another rebel, Basilakes. In Asia another rival, Nikephoros Melissenos, rose with Turkish troops and let them into the towns he took. In Italy, Robert Guiscard was furious: Botaneiates had broken off his daughter's match with Michael VII's son.

Guiscard got ready to invade, with a man claiming to be Michael VII. In February 1081 the Komnenos brothers, Isaac and Alexios, fled the capital and raised the army, with the Doukas family on their side. On 1 April 1081 they got in through a gate held by German mercenaries, and their troops looted the city. Botaneiates abdicated and became a monk.

claims.text: Robert Guiscard brought along a man claiming to be the deposed Michael VII.
claims.note: Anna Komnene says the pretender was a monk named Raiktor. Other sources agree there was a fake. Anna mocks him, so the details are coloured.

claims.text: Maria of Alania secretly backed the Komnenos coup.
claims.note: Anna Komnene, who had good reason to flatter the family, hints at it. Maria did adopt Alexios as a son.

claims.text: As a monk, Botaneiates said the only thing he minded was giving up meat.
claims.note: A later chronicler's anecdote, told to show how lightly he let go of power.

reigns.hook: Botaneiates is in a monastery. The new emperor is a soldier of about 24 with an empty treasury, and Robert Guiscard's Normans are about to land.

reigns.tagline: He called for help and got the First Crusade
reigns.cameToPower: Military coup with his brother Isaac
reigns.previously: Botaneiates gives up. The Komnenos brothers' troops loot the city.
paragraphs: Alexios was a soldier from a great family, and his first year was a disaster. Robert Guiscard and his son Bohemond crushed him at Dyrrhachion in October 1081. To get a fleet he gave Venice tax-free trade across the empire, a deal his heirs would regret. He left the government to his formidable mother, Anna Dalassene, and kept fighting. In 1091 he wiped out the Pecheneg nomads at Levounion.

Then he asked Pope Urban II for western soldiers. He got far more than he wanted: the First Crusade, tens of thousands of knights and pilgrims arriving in 1096–1097. Alexios made their leaders swear oaths to hand back old Roman cities, and shipped them across to Asia. Bohemond kept Antioch for himself, and the bad blood lasted for generations.

He also burned the heretic Basil the Bogomil in the Hippodrome. His daughter Anna later wrote his life, the Alexiad. As he lay dying in August 1118, his wife Irene and Anna pressed him to choose Anna's husband, Nikephoros Bryennios. Alexios kept his son John.

claims.text: Dying Alexios slipped his ring to his son John, signalling him to grab the throne.
claims.note: Told by Niketas Choniates, writing decades later. Other versions say John simply took the ring.

claims.text: Alexios gave Venice its trade privileges in 1082.
claims.note: The charter survives only in later copies. Many historians date it 1082; some argue for 1092.

claims.text: Alexios begged the West for help in a desperate letter to Count Robert of Flanders.
claims.note: The letter exists but is widely thought to be a forgery or heavy rewrite, made to drum up crusaders.

reigns.hook: Alexios is dead, and the palace is a nest of plotters. His daughter Anna has her own candidate for the throne. Her brother John moves first, and Anna starts to scheme.

reigns.tagline: The kindest emperor, killed by his own arrow
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the palace as his father died
reigns.previously: Alexios I dies, and John beats his sister Anna to the throne.
paragraphs: John was very dark-skinned and plain, and people called him Kaloïoannes, John the Good. Within a year his sister Anna was caught plotting against him. He took her property, then gave it back. He spent his reign on campaign: he crushed the Pechenegs in 1122, fought the Hungarians and Serbs, and lost a trade war with Venice, which had raided his islands until he renewed its privileges.

In 1137 he marched into Cilicia and made Raymond, the crusader prince of Antioch, submit to him. With his wife Irene he founded the great Pantokrator monastery in Constantinople, with a hospital attached. In 1143, back in Cilicia and planning to go further, he was hunting a boar when he cut his hand on one of his own arrows. The wound turned bad.
Two of his elder sons had already died. Dying, John passed over his son Isaac, who was in the capital, and named his youngest son, Manuel, who was with him in the army.

claims.text: John never had anyone put to death or mutilated during his reign.
claims.note: Niketas Choniates says so, and no executions are recorded. He admired John, so it is praise as well as fact.

claims.text: The poisoned-arrow wound was a murder disguised as an accident.
claims.note: Choniates tells it as an accident. Some historians suspect a plot by soldiers who favoured his son Isaac; there is no proof.

claims.text: John appears in the Hagia Sophia mosaic as he really looked.
claims.note: The mosaic is from his lifetime, but Byzantine portraits followed set types. It still gives him a long, dark face.

reigns.hook: John names his youngest son, Manuel, in an army camp far from home. But the elder brother, Isaac, is in the capital, close to the treasury. Manuel has to get there first.

reigns.tagline: The knight emperor who dreamed of one Rome
reigns.previously: John II dies in Cilicia and names his youngest son, Manuel.
paragraphs: Manuel was dashing and liked western ways. He married two westerners, Bertha of Sulzbach and later Maria of Antioch, and he jousted with crusader knights. The Second Crusade came through in 1147 under the kings of Germany and France, and everyone parted angry. In 1155 he tried to win back southern Italy, and by 1156 the attempt had failed.

In the East he made the crusader states bow. In 1158 Raynald of Châtillon, who had ravaged Byzantine Cyprus, came to Manuel at Mopsuestia barefoot and bareheaded to beg forgiveness. Manuel beat Hungary in 1167. On 12 March 1171 he had every Venetian in the empire arrested in a single day.

Then in 1176 he marched against the Seljuks and was ambushed in a mountain pass at Myriokephalon. He got most of his army home, but his dream of retaking Anatolia was over. He died in September 1180. His son Alexios II was only eleven.

claims.text: Manuel compared Myriokephalon to Manzikert himself.
claims.note: Choniates says Manuel likened the two defeats. Manuel's own letter to Henry II of England, which plays it down, survives too.

claims.text: Manuel trusted astrologers, even on his deathbed.
claims.note: Choniates says Manuel's astrologers promised he would recover, and he believed them until near the end.

claims.text: Manuel rode in a tournament at Antioch and outshone the crusader knights.
claims.note: Told by Choniates and other admirers; a nice story of a Greek emperor beating Latins at their own game.

reigns.hook: An eleven-year-old emperor, a foreign mother who rules for him, a court full of resentful cousins. And out on the Black Sea coast, Manuel's old rival Andronikos is watching.

In 1182 Manuel's cousin Andronikos marched on the city amid a massacre of its Latin residents. He made himself co-emperor and in 1183 had the boy strangled, then married his 12-year-old widow.

reigns.tagline: The charming rogue who ruled by terror
reigns.cameToPower: Marched on the city; had the boy killed
reigns.previously: Manuel I dies. His son Alexios II is eleven.
paragraphs: The boy Alexios II (1180–1183) was ruled for by his Latin mother, Maria of Antioch, and the city hated her foreign friends. Enter Andronikos, Manuel's cousin, a famous seducer and escape artist who had run off with royal women, broken out of prison and wandered from Kiev to Muslim courts. In 1182 he marched on the capital, and the Latins of Constantinople were massacred.

Maria was condemned and strangled. In 1183 Andronikos made himself co-emperor, then had the boy killed. In his sixties, he married Alexios's twelve-year-old widow, Agnes of France. He went after corrupt officials and greedy nobles with real zeal, and his terror turned into a habit. Blindings and executions filled his reign.

In August 1185 the Normans sacked Thessalonica. When Andronikos's men came to arrest a nobleman, Isaac Angelos, Isaac killed their leader and ran to Hagia Sophia. The crowd rose. Andronikos tried to flee by sea and was caught, and the mob tortured him for days before killing him in the Hippodrome.

claims.text: Alexios II was strangled with a bowstring and his body thrown into the sea.
claims.note: Choniates gives the details. He served in the government and despised Andronikos, but the murder is not in doubt.

claims.text: The mob broke his teeth, cut off his hand, gouged an eye, and paraded him on a mangy camel.
claims.note: Choniates describes it at length, writing as a witness to the period. Some details may be heightened.

claims.text: A prophecy that a name starting with "I" would take his throne drove Andronikos to hunt Isaac.
claims.note: Choniates tells the omen story. It fits Isaac's name too neatly to trust.

reigns.hook: The crowd in Hagia Sophia has a new emperor, a nobleman who killed a man that morning. Isaac Angelos did not plan this. He has no idea how to run an empire.

reigns.tagline: Crowned by a mob, blinded by his brother
reigns.previously: Andronikos I is torn apart by a mob in the Hippodrome.
paragraphs: Isaac Angelos started well. His general Alexios Branas threw the Normans out of the Balkans in November 1185. Then a tax for his wedding to a Hungarian princess pushed the Vlachs and Bulgarians too far. Two brothers, Peter and Asen, rose in revolt, and by 1186 they had founded a new Bulgarian kingdom.

In 1189 the German emperor Frederick Barbarossa marched through on the Third Crusade. Isaac jailed his envoys and tried to slow him down. Barbarossa took Philippopolis and threatened Constantinople, and Isaac gave in and ferried him to Asia. At home Isaac spent lavishly on palaces and favourites.

On 8 April 1195, while Isaac was out hunting in Thrace, his older brother Alexios had himself proclaimed emperor. Isaac was caught and blinded. His young son, also called Alexios, was kept at court and later escaped to the West.

claims.text: The Bulgarian revolt began after Isaac squeezed the Vlachs to pay for his wedding.
claims.note: Choniates says so. The brothers also had a grudge after being snubbed at court.

claims.text: Isaac's own brother, whom he had ransomed from captivity in Saladin's lands, overthrew him.
claims.note: Choniates notes the ingratitude; Isaac had paid to free Alexios.

claims.text: The rebel brothers had wild-eyed prophets proclaim that God wanted the Bulgarians free.
claims.note: Choniates tells it with scorn. It may record real revival preaching, seen through a hostile eye.

reigns.hook: Isaac sits blind in a cell. His brother, now Alexios III, has the throne. But the boy who slipped away is knocking on doors in the West, and he is offering a fortune for an army.

reigns.tagline: He robbed the dead and fled with the gold
reigns.previously: Isaac II is blinded by his own brother while out hunting.
paragraphs: Alexios III was idle and easily led, and many said his clever wife, Euphrosyne, really ran things. When the German emperor Henry VI demanded a huge payment, Alexios raised a special tax and broke into the imperial tombs for their gold. Henry died in 1197 before most of it was paid.

His nephew, Isaac's son Alexios, escaped to the West. He found the knights of the Fourth Crusade camped with a Venetian fleet and short of cash, and promised them 200,000 marks and help for the crusade if they put his father back on the throne.

The fleet arrived off Constantinople in June 1203. On 17 July the crusaders attacked; the Venetians took part of the sea walls and set fires. Alexios III led his army out, then pulled back without a fight. That night he fled, taking a daughter and a fortune in gold and jewels.

claims.text: Euphrosyne largely governed the empire for her husband.
claims.note: Niketas Choniates, who was in office then, says so. His portrait of her is openly hostile.

claims.text: Alexios stripped gold and gems from the tombs of earlier emperors to pay the Germans.
claims.note: Choniates says only Constantine the Great's tomb was spared. He saw the money being raised.

claims.text: He fled with about ten kentenaria of gold and a bag of jewels.
claims.note: Choniates gives the figure. Amounts in chronicles are rough, but the flight with treasure is not doubted.

reigns.hook: By morning the emperor is gone. Courtiers fetch blind Isaac II from his cell and sit him back on the throne. The crusaders want his son Alexios beside him, and their 200,000 marks.

reigns.title: Isaac II and Alexios IV
reigns.tagline: A blind father and a broke son, propped up by crusaders
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother and nephew of Alexios III
reigns.previously: Alexios III flees in the night with his gold, jewels and a daughter.
paragraphs: With Alexios III gone, palace officials pulled blind Isaac II out of prison, dressed him in imperial robes and sat him back on the throne. The crusaders camped outside wanted proof that his son's promises would be kept. Isaac agreed, and on 1 August 1203 the young man was crowned in Hagia Sophia as Alexios IV, his father's co-emperor.

The promises were huge: 200,000 silver marks, troops for the crusade and the Greek Church's obedience to Rome. Alexios melted down church silver and still came up short. In August some Westerners attacked a mosque in the city and started a fire that burned through a vast stretch of Constantinople. Greeks now hated the crusaders, and Alexios with them.

He stopped paying. The crusaders sent him an ultimatum, and in January 1204 the Greeks launched fireships at the Venetian fleet. Old Isaac grew bitter and jealous of his son. On 25 January a crowd in Hagia Sophia chose a reluctant young noble, Nicholas Kanabos, as emperor. Days later the courtier Alexios Doukas seized Alexios IV in the night and threw him into a cell.

claims.text: Alexios IV paid the crusaders only part of what he promised.
claims.note: Villehardouin and Choniates agree that the money ran short. Roughly half seems to have been paid.

claims.text: Blind Isaac listened to astrologers who told him he would see again and rule the world.
claims.note: Choniates tells this to mock the old emperor. He was a hostile witness.

claims.text: Alexios IV was strangled after attempts to poison him failed.
claims.note: Choniates and Western chroniclers give different details of the murder, but agree it was ordered by Mourtzouphlos.

reigns.hook: Alexios IV sits in a cell and old Isaac is dying. The man holding the keys is the courtier Mourtzouphlos, and he is about to crown himself.

reigns.tagline: The bushy-browed emperor who lost Constantinople
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the palace in a coup
reigns.reignEnded: Fled as the crusaders broke in
reigns.previously: Alexios IV is thrown into a cell by his own courtier.
paragraphs: Alexios Doukas was called Mourtzouphlos, probably for his thick eyebrows that met in the middle. Alexios IV had freed him from prison and made him a top palace official. He repaid him by seizing him, and on 5 February 1204 had himself crowned. A few days later Alexios IV was strangled in his cell, and old Isaac died around the same time.

Mourtzouphlos was the only fighter the city had left. He refused the crusaders' demands, built up the walls and led a sortie, though he lost a precious icon of the Virgin to the enemy. On 9 April he beat off their first assault. On 12 April they broke through the sea walls on the Golden Horn, and that night he fled with Alexios III's wife and daughter.

For three days the crusaders looted. Churches were stripped, and the four bronze horses of the Hippodrome were shipped to Venice. On 16 May Baldwin of Flanders was crowned Latin emperor. Mourtzouphlos joined Alexios III in Thrace and married his daughter, but his father-in-law had him blinded. Caught by the crusaders, he was thrown to his death from the Column of Theodosius.

claims.text: During the sack, crusaders sat a prostitute on the patriarch's throne in Hagia Sophia, where she sang bawdy songs and danced.
claims.note: Told by Niketas Choniates, who lived through the sack and lost his house in it. No other witness describes the scene.

claims.text: The crusaders captured an icon of the Virgin from Mourtzouphlos in a skirmish.
claims.note: Both Villehardouin and Robert of Clari, who were with the crusaders, describe the prize being paraded.

claims.text: He was executed by being thrown from the top of the Column of Theodosius.
claims.note: Greek and Western writers agree on this public death, staged as punishment for killing Alexios IV.

reigns.hook: Mourtzouphlos is gone and the city is a ruin. In the wreckage, Alexios III's son-in-law Theodore Laskaris slips across to Asia Minor and starts building an empire in exile.

reigns.tagline: The refugee who built an empire across the water
reigns.previously: Mourtzouphlos flees, the crusaders sack the city, a Latin is crowned.
paragraphs: Theodore Laskaris had married Anna, a daughter of Alexios III, and fought in the doomed defence of the city. After the sack he crossed into Asia Minor and gathered refugees, soldiers and anyone else who would follow him, with Nicaea as his base. His was not the only Byzantine state left. A relative of the Angeloi set himself up in Epirus in the west, and two grandsons of Andronikos I founded a little empire of their own at Trebizond on the Black Sea.

The Latins were dangerous neighbours, but they had troubles too. In 1205 the Bulgarians smashed them at Adrianople and captured Emperor Baldwin I, who never came home. His brother Henry, far more able, took over and pushed Theodore hard. In 1208 a new patriarch, elected at Nicaea, crowned Theodore emperor. That gave the exiles a real emperor and a real Church.

In 1211 the Seljuk sultan invaded, with Theodore's old father-in-law Alexios III in tow. At Antioch on the Maeander the Seljuks were beaten and the sultan was killed. Alexios III was captured and shut away in a monastery. Theodore died in 1221 with no surviving son, and left the crown to his daughter Irene's husband, John Vatatzes.

claims.text: Theodore killed the Seljuk sultan with his own hands at Antioch on the Maeander.
claims.note: George Akropolites tells it as single combat between the two rulers. Other accounts just say the sultan fell in the fighting.

claims.text: Baldwin I died a prisoner of the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan.
claims.note: He vanished into Bulgarian captivity in 1205. How he died is unknown, and the grisly stories that spread later are unproven.

reigns.hook: Theodore's brothers think the crown should be theirs, and they've gone over to the Latins. John Vatatzes is about to meet them on the battlefield.

reigns.tagline: The farmer-emperor who bought a crown with eggs
reigns.previously: Theodore I dies with no son and leaves Nicaea to his son-in-law.
paragraphs: John Vatatzes started by beating Theodore's brothers, who had joined the Latins, at Poimanenon in 1224. Then he kept on winning. He took back almost all the Latin lands in Asia Minor, crossed into Europe and in 1246 took Thessalonica. The Latin emperors in Constantinople, Robert and then Baldwin II, were left with little more than the city itself, kept afloat by handouts from the West.

At home he was a careful manager. He ran the imperial estates like a model farm and told his people to buy home-grown goods instead of foreign luxuries. Luck helped too. In 1243 the Mongols crushed the Seljuks, taking the pressure off his eastern border. After his first wife Irene died, he married Constance, a young daughter of the German emperor Frederick II, who took the Greek name Anna.

He suffered from epilepsy, and the fits got worse in his last years. He died at Nymphaion in November 1254, and his son Theodore took over. The Orthodox Church later made John a saint, and Greeks still remember him as John the Merciful.

claims.text: John bought his empress a jewelled crown with the money from selling eggs from the imperial farms.
claims.note: Nikephoros Gregoras tells it about a century later, as a lesson in thrift. It sounds like a moral tale, but his estates really were run for profit.

claims.text: John's affair with his young wife's Italian lady-in-waiting scandalised the court.
claims.note: The scholar Nikephoros Blemmydes wrote about it and barred the woman from his church. George Akropolites mentions it too.

claims.text: John III is venerated as a saint.
claims.note: A local cult grew up around Magnesia soon after his death, and he is honoured in the Orthodox Church as John the Merciful.

reigns.hook: John's son Theodore is a brilliant scholar with a short temper, his father's illness and a deep distrust of the great noble families. They feel the same about him.

reigns.tagline: A philosopher on the throne, with a temper to match
reigns.previously: John III, the Merciful, dies at Nymphaion after 33 years.
paragraphs: Theodore had been taught by the finest scholar in the empire, Nikephoros Blemmydes, and he never stopped writing: theology, essays and sharp, clever letters. He took the surname of his mother's family, Laskaris. As emperor he fought two hard campaigns against the Bulgarians and won back the land they had grabbed when his father died.

He didn't trust the great aristocratic families, and they didn't trust him. He gave top jobs to men of modest birth, above all George Mouzalon and his brothers, and treated proud nobles harshly. Michael Palaiologos, a dashing young general, decided he was safer abroad and fled to the Seljuks for a while. Theodore's illness kept getting worse, and he died in August 1258 at about 36.

He left his son John IV, aged seven, with George Mouzalon as regent. The nobles loathed Mouzalon. Only days after Theodore's death, at a memorial service for the emperor, soldiers burst in and cut Mouzalon and his brothers down.

claims.text: Michael Palaiologos was behind the murder of the regent George Mouzalon.
claims.note: George Akropolites and George Pachymeres describe the killing. Michael gained most from it, and suspicion fell on him, but nothing was proved.

claims.text: Theodore's illness was epilepsy, like his father's.
claims.note: Writers at the time describe fits and collapses. Modern historians usually call it epilepsy, but nobody can diagnose him now.

reigns.hook: A seven-year-old emperor, a murdered regent and a charming general back from exile. The nobles know exactly who they want in charge: Michael Palaiologos.

paragraphs: John IV was seven when he became emperor at Nicaea. His regent was murdered within days, and the nobleman Michael Palaiologos took over as regent and then co-emperor.

After Michael's men retook Constantinople in 1261, he was crowned there alone. On Christmas Day 1261, John's eleventh birthday, Michael had him blinded and locked in a fortress, where he lived for over 40 more years.

reigns.tagline: He won back Constantinople almost by accident
reigns.cameToPower: Made co-emperor, then blinded John IV
reigns.previously: Theodore II dies, and his hated regent is murdered at the memorial.
paragraphs: Michael Palaiologos made himself regent for the boy John IV, then co-emperor on 1 January 1259. That year his army beat an alliance of Epirus, Sicily and the crusader prince of Achaea at Pelagonia. In March 1261, at Nymphaion, he signed a treaty with Genoa for a war fleet. He never needed it. That July his general Alexios Strategopoulos, passing Constantinople with a small force, found it barely guarded and slipped inside.

Baldwin II, the last Latin emperor, fled. On 15 August 1261 Michael walked into the city on foot, behind the holy icon of the Virgin Hodegetria. Then, on Christmas Day, John IV's eleventh birthday, Michael had the boy blinded. Patriarch Arsenios excommunicated him for it, and a bitter church quarrel followed.

The big danger was Charles of Anjou, the French king of Sicily, who wanted Constantinople for himself. Michael bought the pope's protection by accepting the Union of Lyon in 1274, which his own people hated. In 1282 the Sicilian Vespers revolt wrecked Charles's plans. Michael died that December on campaign, and the Church refused him a proper funeral.

claims.text: Constantinople was retaken almost by accident, by a small force that found the city unguarded.
claims.note: Akropolites and Pachymeres tell it this way: the Latin fleet was away and locals helped the men in. Historians accept the outline but argue over how planned it was.

claims.text: Michael paid for the Sicilian Vespers, and boasted of it in his memoir.
claims.note: His autobiography says God freed the Sicilians through his hand. How much Byzantine gold actually reached the rebels is still debated.

claims.text: John IV was blinded on his eleventh birthday.
claims.note: Pachymeres tells the story. John lived on for decades in a fortress in Bithynia, where Michael's son Andronikos II later visited him.

reigns.hook: Michael's son Andronikos inherits the old capital, a furious Church and an army and navy the treasury can no longer pay for.

reigns.tagline: The pious emperor who scrapped the fleet
reigns.previously: Michael VIII dies in Thrace and is refused a church funeral.
paragraphs: Andronikos began by tearing up his father's hated union with Rome, which pleased nearly everyone. Then he cut costs. He laid up the fleet, leaned on hired Genoese ships and trimmed the army. Meanwhile a Turkish chief called Osman was raiding in Bithynia, and in 1302 he beat a Byzantine force at Bapheus. The Ottomans had arrived. At court, the minister Theodore Metochites paid for the glowing mosaics of the Chora church.

In 1303 Andronikos hired the Catalan Company, tough Spanish mercenaries led by Roger de Flor. They beat the Turks, then turned on their employers. When Roger was murdered in 1305 at the court of Andronikos's son and co-emperor, Michael IX, the Catalans took their revenge by ravaging Thrace for years. Michael IX died in 1320.

Andronikos's grandson and namesake was wild and spoiled. After the young man's men killed his own brother Manuel, the old emperor disinherited him, and from 1321 the two fought a string of civil wars. Bursa fell to the Ottomans in 1326. In May 1328 the grandson took Constantinople. Andronikos II became a monk and died in 1332.

claims.text: Young Andronikos's men killed his brother Manuel by mistake, while lying in wait for a rival in love.
claims.note: Nikephoros Gregoras tells the story and says the shock helped kill their father, Michael IX. It makes a good tale; the details can't be checked.

claims.text: Scrapping the navy left the empire at the mercy of Genoa and Venice.
claims.note: Gregoras and later historians blame Andronikos. Others point out the treasury was empty and he had little choice.

claims.text: Theodore Metochites appears in a Chora mosaic, offering the church to Christ.
claims.note: The mosaic survives in the Kariye Mosque in Istanbul.

reigns.hook: The grandson has won. Andronikos III is young, charming and loves hunting. Luckily his best friend, John Kantakouzenos, loves paperwork.

reigns.tagline: The playboy whose best friend ran the empire
reigns.cameToPower: Beat his grandfather in civil war
reigns.previously: Andronikos II loses to his grandson and ends his days as a monk.
paragraphs: Andronikos III liked hunting, jousting and parties far more than paperwork. Luckily his friend John Kantakouzenos was happy to run the government. They had their work cut out, because the Ottomans under Orhan were swallowing what was left of Byzantine Asia Minor. In 1329 Andronikos marched to relieve Nicaea and was wounded at Pelekanon, and his army fell back in confusion.

Nicaea fell in 1331 and Nicomedia in 1337. In the Aegean and the Balkans things went better. He won Chios back from the Genoese in 1329 and brought Epirus back under Byzantine rule. At home he named four 'universal judges' to clean up the courts. His second wife was an Italian princess, Anna of Savoy.

Near the end of his reign a fierce church fight broke out over the hesychasts, monks led by Gregory Palamas who said prayer could let them see God's uncreated light. Andronikos chaired a council on it in June 1341, which backed Palamas, and died days later, aged 44. His son John V was three days short of nine.

claims.text: Kantakouzenos was the real ruler while Andronikos enjoyed himself.
claims.note: Our fullest account is Kantakouzenos's own history, which casts him as the indispensable friend. He was hardly a neutral witness.

claims.text: The council of June 1341 backed Gregory Palamas.
claims.note: The council's decision and later councils of 1347 and 1351 confirmed the hesychasts' teaching.

reigns.hook: An eight-year-old emperor, his mother, a scheming admiral and the dead emperor's best friend. Byzantium is about to tear itself apart.

reigns.tagline: Fifty years on the throne, most of them in trouble
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a boy
reigns.previously: Andronikos III dies at 44, leaving an heir just short of nine.
paragraphs: John V's mother Anna of Savoy, the patriarch and the ambitious Alexios Apokaukos took charge and shut out Kantakouzenos. He claimed the throne, and civil war raged from 1341 to 1347. Apokaukos was lynched by political prisoners in 1345 while inspecting a new prison. In 1347 Kantakouzenos won, became senior emperor and married his daughter Helena to John. In 1354 the Ottomans took Gallipoli, and by the end of that year John V was back in charge.

He spent the rest of his life hunting for help. Coming home from Hungary in 1366, he was held up by the Bulgarians at Vidin. In 1369 he became a Catholic in Rome, and on the way back Venice detained him over his debts. In the end he became the sultan's vassal.

His son Andronikos IV rebelled with the sultan's son in 1373 and was blinded on Murad's orders, along with his own small son John. In 1376 Andronikos seized the throne and jailed his father and brother Manuel until 1379. In 1390 the grandson, John VII, held the city for five months. John V died in February 1391.

claims.text: Andronikos IV and his little son were only partly blinded, keeping some sight.
claims.note: Murad demanded the blinding. Byzantine writers say both kept some vision, perhaps because the job was done half-heartedly on purpose.

claims.text: Venice held John V as a debtor until his son Manuel raised the money.
claims.note: Chroniclers tell it this way. How formal the detention was is unclear.

claims.text: Bayezid made John tear down his new fortifications by threatening to blind Manuel.
claims.note: Told by the historian Doukas, writing decades later. Manuel was serving at the Ottoman court at the time.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 1341. The man shut out of the regency is Andronikos III's best friend, John Kantakouzenos, and he isn't going quietly.

reigns.tagline: Kingmaker, then king, then monk
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival and father-in-law of John V
reigns.previously: John V's regents shut out Kantakouzenos, and civil war begins.
paragraphs: John Kantakouzenos was rich, clever and Andronikos III's closest friend. Shut out of the regency, he had himself proclaimed emperor at Didymoteichon on 26 October 1341. The civil war that followed was savage. He hired Turkish allies, first Umur of Aydin and then the Ottoman ruler Orhan, who married his daughter Theodora in 1346. In Thessalonica a radical party, the Zealots, threw out the rich and ran the city themselves until 1350.

Kantakouzenos took Constantinople in February 1347 and ruled as senior emperor beside young John V, who married his daughter Helena. Then the Black Death arrived and killed his youngest son, Andronikos. He backed Gregory Palamas and the hesychast monks, and church councils confirmed their teaching.

His Turkish allies didn't leave. They took the fort of Tzympe near Gallipoli, and when an earthquake wrecked Gallipoli's walls in 1354, they moved in. The city turned against him. In December 1354 he abdicated and became the monk Joasaph. He lived almost 30 more years and wrote a history of his times, starring himself. He died in the Morea in 1383.

claims.text: Kantakouzenos never wanted the throne and was pushed into claiming it.
claims.note: That is how his own history tells it. Gregoras, who knew him, is less kind, and historians read his memoir as a defence of his record.

claims.text: Orhan married Kantakouzenos's daughter Theodora in 1346.
claims.note: Kantakouzenos describes the wedding himself. Theodora stayed a Christian and later helped Christians in Ottoman lands.

claims.text: The 1354 earthquake let the Ottomans walk into Gallipoli.
claims.note: Several sources link the two: the townspeople fled the ruins and the Turks moved in and rebuilt.

reigns.hook: Back to 1391. John V is dead, and his son Manuel is a hostage at the Ottoman court. He has to get home before anyone else grabs the throne.

reigns.previously: John V is a vassal of the Ottomans, and his son rebels.
paragraphs: Andronikos had already tried to overthrow his father once and been partly blinded for it. In 1376, with Genoese and Ottoman support, he took Constantinople and imprisoned John V.
He paid the Ottomans by handing them Gallipoli. In 1379 John V escaped and returned with Ottoman and Venetian help, and Andronikos fled, though he kept lands on the Sea of Marmara.
reigns.hook: John V is back on his throne, still paying tribute to the Ottomans.

reigns.tagline: The grandson who seized the city
reigns.previously: Andronikos IV's son wants his father's throne.
paragraphs: John VII, the son of Andronikos IV, seized Constantinople from his grandfather John V in April 1390 with backing from the Ottoman sultan Bayezid.
His uncle Manuel drove him out after five months. The two were later reconciled, and John VII governed Constantinople as regent while Manuel toured Europe begging for help against the Ottomans.
reigns.hook: John V is restored, but only for a few months more.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who spent Christmas in Eltham
reigns.reignEnded: Died a monk after a stroke
reigns.previously: Kantakouzenos becomes a monk. In 1391 old John V dies too.
paragraphs: Manuel slipped away from Bayezid's court and reached Constantinople before anyone could stop him. He was still the sultan's vassal and had to ride on Ottoman campaigns. Then Bayezid turned on the city and blockaded it from 1394. A big Western crusade came to help and was crushed at Nicopolis in 1396.

In 1399 Manuel left his nephew John VII in charge and toured Western Europe asking for help. He was learned, dignified and made a great impression. He stayed in Paris and spent Christmas 1400 as Henry IV's guest at Eltham Palace in England. He got feasts and promises and little else. Then, in 1402, Timur crushed Bayezid at Ankara, and the siege was over.

Manuel backed Mehmed I in the Ottoman civil war that followed and won years of peace. In 1415 he built the Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth. Under Murad II the pressure came back, with a siege in 1422. Manuel had a stroke, became the monk Matthew and died in 1425. Centuries later his dialogue with a Persian Muslim scholar was quoted by Pope Benedict XVI, causing uproar.

claims.text: Manuel spent Christmas 1400 with Henry IV of England at Eltham.
claims.note: English chroniclers record the visit, and Manuel wrote home about his welcome in England.

claims.text: Pope Benedict XVI quoted Manuel's words on Islam in a 2006 lecture.
claims.note: The Regensburg lecture of September 2006 caused protests across the Muslim world; the pope later said the words were not his own view.

claims.text: Manuel advised his son to keep talking about church union but never actually agree to it.
claims.note: Reported by George Sphrantzes, a courtier who knew both men. It fits Manuel's caution, but it's one witness.

reigns.hook: Manuel's son John VIII inherits a city ringed by Ottoman land. He thinks the answer lies in Italy, with the pope, and he's willing to pay the price.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who bet everything on Rome
reigns.previously: Manuel II dies a monk after decades of asking for help.
paragraphs: John VIII had seen one great city go already. Thessalonica, besieged by the Ottomans, was handed to Venice in 1423, and Murad II took it anyway in 1430. John decided only the West could save Constantinople, and the West's price was church union.

In 1437 he sailed to Italy with the patriarch and hundreds of churchmen. At the Council of Ferrara-Florence they argued for months, and on 6 July 1439 the union of the Latin and Greek churches was proclaimed. The artist Pisanello sketched the emperor's tall hat and pointed beard and made a medal of him. Back home, most clergy and ordinary people rejected the deal.

The crusade it bought marched in 1444 and was destroyed at Varna. John died in October 1448 with no children, though he had married three times. His mother, Helena Dragaš, made sure the throne went to his brother Constantine.

claims.text: 'Better the Turkish turban than the Latin mitre.'
claims.note: The historian Doukas puts the words in the mouth of the grand duke Loukas Notaras, just before the fall. They sum up the anti-union mood, whoever said them.

claims.text: Pisanello's medal of John VIII was the first Renaissance portrait medal.
claims.note: It is often called the first, and it started a fashion. There are earlier medal-like pieces, so 'first' is arguable.

claims.text: The union of the churches was proclaimed in Florence on 6 July 1439.
claims.note: The decree survives, signed in Latin and Greek.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is far away at Mistra, in the Peloponnese. Across the Bosporus, a young man named Mehmed is about to become sultan, and he has one goal.

reigns.tagline: The last emperor went down with his city
reigns.previously: John VIII dies childless, and his mother picks Constantine.
paragraphs: Constantine was Despot of the Morea, ruling from Mistra, when he was proclaimed emperor there on 6 January 1449. In 1451 the 18-year-old Mehmed II became sultan, and in 1452 he built a great fortress, Rumeli Hisarı, on the European shore of the Bosporus to choke the city's supplies. On 12 December 1452, hoping to win help from the West, Constantine had the church union proclaimed in Hagia Sophia.

The siege began on 6 April 1453. A few thousand defenders, Greeks, Venetians and Genoese, faced a huge army with giant cannon cast by an engineer called Orban. A chain blocked the Golden Horn, so on 22 April Mehmed had ships dragged overland on rollers into it. For weeks the guns pounded the walls.

In the early hours of 29 May the final assault came. The Genoese commander Giovanni Giustiniani was badly wounded and carried off, and the defence crumbled. Constantine was last seen fighting near the walls. The Roman Empire, which had lasted in some form for nearly 1,500 years, was over.

claims.text: The Turks got in through a small gate, the Kerkoporta, that had been left open.
claims.note: Told by the historian Doukas. Many historians think it played a small part at most, next to the collapse after Giustiniani was hit.

claims.text: Constantine's body was never surely identified.
claims.note: Some accounts say his head was shown to Mehmed, others that he was found by his purple boots. No grave was ever known.

claims.text: An angel turned Constantine to marble and hid him under the city, and one day he will wake and take it back.
claims.note: The Marble Emperor is a Greek folk legend that grew up after the fall.
